Let $a=\sqrt{x-1},\,b=\sqrt{y-1},\,c=\sqrt{z-1}\ge0$. By symmetry assume the minimum is attained at the $z$-term, i.e. $z\le x,y$ (so $c\le a,b$). The equation becomes
$$\sqrt{(c^2+1)\bigl(1+(a^2+1)(b^2+1)\bigr)}=a+b+c.$$
Squaring and simplifying yields a quadratic in $c$:
$$(a^2+1)(b^2+1)c^2-2(a+b)c+\bigl((ab-1)^2+1\bigr)=0.$$
Its discriminant is
$$\Delta=4(a+b)^2-4(a^2+1)(b^2+1)\bigl((ab-1)^2+1\bigr)=-4(ab-1)^2\bigl(a^2+b^2+a^2b^2+2\bigr)\le0.$$
Since $c$ is real, $\Delta=0$, forcing $ab=1$ and $c=\frac{a+b}{(a^2+1)(b^2+1)}=\frac1{a+b}$.
Thus $(x-1)(y-1)=1$ and
$$z=c^2+1=1+\frac1{(a+b)^2}=1+\frac1{x+y},$$
using $(a+b)^2=x-1+y-1+2\sqrt{(x-1)(y-1)}=x+y$. Since $a,b>0$, we have $c<a,b$, so $z=\min(x,y,z)$ holds automatically. No solutions exist with ties at the minimum (they lead to contradictions like $x=-1$). By symmetry, all solutions are permutations of such triples. Setting $t=x-1>0$ gives $y=1+\frac1t$ and $z=1+\frac{t}{(t+1)^2}$.

\boxed{\text{All permutations of }\left(t+1,\ 1+\dfrac{1}{t},\ 1+\dfrac{t}{(t+1)^2}\right)\text{ where }t>0.}
